claim: µ-opioid receptors (µORs) are widely expressed throughout the peripheral and central parts of the nociceptive system and strongly control neuronal excitation.
source: Throughout the peripheral and central parts of the nociceptive system, µ-opioid receptors (µORs) are widely expressed and strongly control neuronal excitation (Stein, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stein, 2016, which is a reference to published scholarly work.

claim: Agonists of µORs are the most potent analgesic drugs clinically available.
source: Agonists of µORs are the most potent analgesic drugs clinically available (Pasternak and Pan, 2013) and are therefore often prescribed for the treatment of severe pain.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pasternak and Pan, 2013.

claim: Opioid substances are especially effective against acute pain states, such as post-operative pain.
source: These opioid substances are especially effective against acute pain states, such as post-operative pain, but they are also used, more controversially, for the treatment of longer lasting or chronic pain (Rowbotham et al., 2003; Chou et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rowbotham et al., 2003 and Chou et al., 2015.

claim: Clinically used opioids cause important unwanted effects, such as addiction, tolerance, opioid-induced hyperalgesia, and respiratory depression.
source: Much of the controversy around opioids arises because these substances cause important unwanted effects, such as addiction, tolerance (Volkow and McLellan, 2016), opioid-induced hyperalgesia (Roeckel et al., 2016) and, when overdosed, respiratory depression (Pattinson, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Volkow and McLellan, 2016; Roeckel et al., 2016; and Pattinson, 2008.

claim: Clinically used opioids are often implicated in fatal overdosing due to drug addiction or dosing accidents.
source: Because of this unfavorable profile of unwanted effects, clinically used opioids are often implicated in fatal overdosing due to drug addiction or dosing accidents (Compton et al., 2016; Ray et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Compton et al., 2016 and Ray et al., 2016.

claim: Opioid receptors are located on the peripheral nerve endings of nociceptor neurons.
source: While many actions of opioids are triggered by activation of µORs in the central nervous system, opioid receptors are also located on the peripheral nerve endings of nociceptor neurons (Stein et al., 1990a, 1990b; Stein, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Stein et al., 1990a, 1990b and Stein, 2013.

claim: In the skin, opioid receptors are targeted by endogenous opioid substances, such as β-endorphin, released from immune cells or skin keratinocytes.
source: Physiologically, in the skin, where many peripheral nociceptor nerve endings reside, opioid receptors are targeted by endogenous opioid substances, such as β-endorphin, released in the periphery from immune cells (Stein et al., 1990b) or skin keratinocytes (Ibrahim et al., 2005; Fell et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Stein et al., 1990b; Ibrahim et al., 2005; and Fell et al., 2014.

claim: Activation of peripheral opioid receptors can provide clinically meaningful analgesia.
source: Activation of peripheral opioid receptors can provide clinically meaningful analgesia (Farley, 2011; Stein and Machelska, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Farley, 2011 and Stein and Machelska, 2011.

claim: Inhibiting peripheral µORs by antagonist application increases pain.
source: On the contrary, inhibiting peripheral µORs by antagonist application increases pain (Jagla et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jagla et al., 2014.

claim: At central synapses, activation of µORs causes inhibition of L-type voltage-gated Ca2+ channels.
source: Activation of µORs causes inhibition of L-type voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (Bourinet et al., 1996; Heinke et al., 2011) and activation of several types of K+ channels (Law et al., 2000; Marker et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bourinet et al., 1996 and Heinke et al., 2011.

claim: At central synapses, activation of µORs causes activation of several types of K+ channels.
source: Activation of µORs causes inhibition of L-type voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (Bourinet et al., 1996; Heinke et al., 2011) and activation of several types of K+ channels (Law et al., 2000; Marker et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Law et al., 2000 and Marker et al., 2005.

claim: At several central synapses, µORs have been shown to interact with TRPV1 channels.
source: Importantly, also at several central synapses, µORs have been shown to interact with TRP channels, notably TRPV1 (recently reviewed by Bao et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bao et al., 2015.

claim: The interaction of TRPV1 and µOR occurs at multiple anatomical locations in the central nervous system and its physiological consequences and mechanisms are highly diverse.
source: The interaction of TRPV1 and µOR occurs at multiple anatomical locations in the central nervous system and its physiological consequences and mechanisms are highly diverse (Maione et al., 2009; Stein, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Maione et al., 2009 and Stein, 2016.

claim: Proposed mechanisms for µOR-TRPV1 interaction range from influencing the cAMP-PKA pathway and the participation of several other kinases (ERK, MAPK, JNK) to β-arrestin2 and the PI3-kinase pathway.
source: Proposed mechanisms range from influencing the cAMP-PKA pathway and the participation of several other kinases (ERK, MAPK, JNK) to β-arrestin2 and the PI3-kinase pathway (Law et al., 2000; Rowan et al., 2014; Bao et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Law et al., 2000; Rowan et al., 2014; and Bao et al., 2015.

claim: In peripheral nerves and their endings, several intracellular signaling events have been proposed to account for the effectiveness of peripherally restricted opioids, including inhibition of voltage-gated Na+ channels.
source: In peripheral nerves and their endings, several, partially different, intracellular signaling events have been proposed to account for the effectiveness of peripherally restricted opioids, including inhibition of voltage-gated Na+ channels (Gold and Levine, 1996), inhibition of HCN channels (Ingram and Williams, 1994), activation of several classes of K+ channels (Cunha et al., 2010; Nockemann et al., 2013; Baillie et al., 2015), and, importantly, again the inhibition of TRPV1 channels (Vetter et al., 2006; Endres-Becker et al., 2007; Spahn et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gold and Levine, 1996.

claim: In peripheral nerves and their endings, several intracellular signaling events have been proposed to account for the effectiveness of peripherally restricted opioids, including inhibition of HCN channels.
source: In peripheral nerves and their endings, several, partially different, intracellular signaling events have been proposed to account for the effectiveness of peripherally restricted opioids, including inhibition of voltage-gated Na+ channels (Gold and Levine, 1996), inhibition of HCN channels (Ingram and Williams, 1994), activation of several classes of K+ channels (Cunha et al., 2010; Nockemann et al., 2013; Baillie et al., 2015), and, importantly, again the inhibition of TRPV1 channels (Vetter et al., 2006; Endres-Becker et al., 2007; Spahn et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ingram and Williams, 1994.

claim: In peripheral nerves and their endings, several intracellular signaling events have been proposed to account for the effectiveness of peripherally restricted opioids, including activation of several classes of K+ channels.
source: In peripheral nerves and their endings, several, partially different, intracellular signaling events have been proposed to account for the effectiveness of peripherally restricted opioids, including inhibition of voltage-gated Na+ channels (Gold and Levine, 1996), inhibition of HCN channels (Ingram and Williams, 1994), activation of several classes of K+ channels (Cunha et al., 2010; Nockemann et al., 2013; Baillie et al., 2015), and, importantly, again the inhibition of TRPV1 channels (Vetter et al., 2006; Endres-Becker et al., 2007; Spahn et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cunha et al., 2010; Nockemann et al., 2013; and Baillie et al., 2015.

claim: In peripheral nerves and their endings, several intracellular signaling events have been proposed to account for the effectiveness of peripherally restricted opioids, including the inhibition of TRPV1 channels.
source: In peripheral nerves and their endings, several, partially different, intracellular signaling events have been proposed to account for the effectiveness of peripherally restricted opioids, including inhibition of voltage-gated Na+ channels (Gold and Levine, 1996), inhibition of HCN channels (Ingram and Williams, 1994), activation of several classes of K+ channels (Cunha et al., 2010; Nockemann et al., 2013; Baillie et al., 2015), and, importantly, again the inhibition of TRPV1 channels (Vetter et al., 2006; Endres-Becker et al., 2007; Spahn et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vetter et al., 2006; Endres-Becker et al., 2007; and Spahn et al., 2013.

claim: TRPM3 channels were described in primary nociceptive neurons.
source: Recently, TRPM3 channels (Oberwinkler and Philipp, 2014) were described in primary nociceptive neurons (Nealen et al., 2003; Lechner et al., 2009; Vriens et al., 2011; Straub et al., 2013a, 2013b; Held et al., 2015; Usoskin et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nealen et al., 2003; Lechner et al., 2009; Vriens et al., 2011; Straub et al., 2013a, 2013b; Held et al., 2015; and Usoskin et al., 2015.

claim: TRPM3 channels are divalent-permeable cation channels.
source: and it was shown that these divalent-permeable cation channels (Grimm et al., 2003; Oberwinkler et al., 2005; Wagner et al., 2010) play an important role in noxious heat sensation since these channels are intrinsically thermosensitive (Vriens et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Grimm et al., 2003; Oberwinkler et al., 2005; and Wagner et al., 2010.

claim: TRPM3 channels play an important role in noxious heat sensation since these channels are intrinsically thermosensitive.
source: and it was shown that these divalent-permeable cation channels (Grimm et al., 2003; Oberwinkler et al., 2005; Wagner et al., 2010) play an important role in noxious heat sensation since these channels are intrinsically thermosensitive (Vriens et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vriens et al., 2011.

claim: Activation of TRPM3 leads to release of pro-inflammatory CGRP from peripheral nociceptor nerve terminals.
source: Activation of TRPM3 leads to release of pro-inflammatory CGRP from peripheral nociceptor nerve terminals (Held et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Held et al., 2015.

claim: TRPM3-deficient animals show severe defects in the development of inflammatory hyperalgesia.
source: while TRPM3-deficient animals show severe defects in the development of inflammatory hyperalgesia (Vriens et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vriens et al., 2011.

claim: Inhibitors of TRPM3 channels have been identified that exhibit strong anti-nociceptive properties.
source: In this context, it is interesting that inhibitors of TRPM3 channels have been identified that exhibit strong anti-nociceptive properties (Straub et al., 2013b; Chen et al., 2014; Suzuki et al., 2016; Krügel et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Straub et al., 2013b; Chen et al., 2014; Suzuki et al., 2016; and Krügel et al., 2017.

claim: Morphine strongly reduced the Ca2+ signals induced by pregnenolone sulfate (PS) in isolated mouse DRG neurons.
source: Testing whether morphine, a traditional agonist of opioid receptors, or its synthetic, µOR-specific analog DAMGO (Handa et al., 1981), influences TRPM3 channel activity, we found that both µOR agonists strongly reduced the Ca2+ signals induced by PS (Figure 1a–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1a-c, which shows experimental measurements of Ca2+ signals.

claim: DAMGO strongly reduced the Ca2+ signals induced by pregnenolone sulfate (PS) in isolated mouse DRG neurons.
source: Testing whether morphine, a traditional agonist of opioid receptors, or its synthetic, µOR-specific analog DAMGO (Handa et al., 1981), influences TRPM3 channel activity, we found that both µOR agonists strongly reduced the Ca2+ signals induced by PS (Figure 1a–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1a-c, which shows experimental measurements of Ca2+ signals.

claim: The reduction of Ca2+ signals by µOR agonists was rapid and readily reversible within a time frame of 1–2 min.
source: The reduction of these Ca2+ signals was rapid and readily reversible within a time frame of 1–2 min (Figure 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1d, which shows the time course of the effect.

claim: Naloxone alone did not affect TRPM3-dependent Ca2+ signals in DRG neurons.
source: Naloxone alone did not affect TRPM3-dependent Ca2+ signals in DRG neurons (Figure 1e,g)
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1e,g, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: When co-applied with DAMGO, naloxone prevented the action of DAMGO completely.
source: but, when co-applied with DAMGO, it prevented the action of DAMGO completely (Figure 1f,g).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1f,g, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: Herkinorin strongly inhibited PS-induced Ca2+ signals in isolated mouse DRG neurons.
source: In addition, we tested two further, structurally different, µOR agonists, herkinorin and loperamide. Both substances strongly inhibited PS-induced Ca2+ signals in isolated mouse DRG neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Loperamide strongly inhibited PS-induced Ca2+ signals in isolated mouse DRG neurons.
source: In addition, we tested two further, structurally different, µOR agonists, herkinorin and loperamide. Both substances strongly inhibited PS-induced Ca2+ signals in isolated mouse DRG neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Activation of µORs, independent of the chemical nature of the agonist, leads to inhibition of TRPM3 channels in DRG neurons.
source: These data indicate that activation of µORs, independent of the chemical nature of the agonist, leads to inhibition of TRPM3 channels in DRG neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that multiple structurally different µOR agonists all inhibit TRPM3 channels.

claim: Morphine inhibited TRPM3-dependent Ca2+ signals in HEK cells overexpressing TRPM3 and µORs.
source: When we overexpressed Gβ1 and Gγ2 proteins together with TRPM3 channels, TRPM3-dependent Ca2+ signals were strongly reduced (Figure 7e).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1h, which shows experimental measurements in HEK cells.

claim: Morphine did not inhibit TRPM3 channels in control cells expressing only TRPM3.
source: Importantly, omitting µOR cDNA from the transfection abolished the effect of morphine (Figure 1h)
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1h, which shows experimental measurements in control cells.

claim: TRPM3 channels activated by the application of nifedipine were inhibited by µOR activation.
source: Taking advantage of the overexpression system, which avoids the complication of other nifedipine- or heat-sensitive conductances (Fajardo et al., 2008; Julius, 2013), we demonstrated that TRPM3 channels activated by the application of nifedipine (Wagner et al., 2008; Drews et al., 2014) or by heat applied in the absence of chemical agonists (Vriens et al., 2011) were also inhibited by µOR activation (Figure 1i,j).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1i, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: TRPM3 channels activated by heat applied in the absence of chemical agonists were inhibited by µOR activation.
source: Taking advantage of the overexpression system, which avoids the complication of other nifedipine- or heat-sensitive conductances (Fajardo et al., 2008; Julius, 2013), we demonstrated that TRPM3 channels activated by the application of nifedipine (Wagner et al., 2008; Drews et al., 2014) or by heat applied in the absence of chemical agonists (Vriens et al., 2011) were also inhibited by µOR activation (Figure 1i,j).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1j, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: Currents through TRPM3 channels were inhibited by activating µORs rapidly in less than 5 s.
source: Whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiological recordings from HEK cells overexpressing TRPM3 and µORs demonstrated that currents through TRPM3 channels were inhibited by activating µORs rapidly in less than 5 s (Figure 1k–m, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1k-m and Figure 1—figure supplement 3, which shows electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The IC50 values for DAMGO-induced inhibition of TRPM3 currents at +80 mV and −80 mV did not differ.
source: After measuring a dose-response curve by varying the concentration of DAMGO, we found that the IC50 values at +80 mV and −80 mV did not differ, providing an indication that inhibition of TRPM3 channels by µOR activation was voltage-independent (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 4, which shows dose-response curves.

claim: Inhibition of TRPM3 channels by µOR activation was voltage-independent.
source: After measuring a dose-response curve by varying the concentration of DAMGO, we found that the IC50 values at +80 mV and −80 mV did not differ, providing an indication that inhibition of TRPM3 channels by µOR activation was voltage-independent (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that IC50 values did not differ at different voltages.

claim: Currents evoked by TRPM3 agonists in isolated DRG neurons were rapidly (less than 5 s) inhibited by µOR activation.
source: Similarly, performing patch-clamp experiments on isolated DRG neurons, we observed that the currents evoked by TRPM3 agonists were rapidly (less than 5 s) inhibited by µOR activation (Figure 2a–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2a-c, which shows electrophysiological recordings from DRG neurons.

claim: Upon washout of DAMGO, the inhibition of TRPM3 currents was at least partially reversible.
source: Upon washout of DAMGO, the inhibition was at least partially reversible.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text.

claim: Application of the µOR agonist DAMGO did not evoke outward currents in isolated DRG neurons.
source: Aiming for small-diameter nociceptors, we selected cells that responded either to TRPV1- or to TRPM3-activating (or to both types of) agonists. In these cells, we could not detect outward currents upon application of the µOR agonist DAMGO (Figure 2d–f).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2d-f, which shows electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The reduction of PS-induced currents by µOR activation is not due to the activation of outward currents.
source: This indicates that the reduction of PS-induced currents by µOR activation is not due to the activation of outward currents.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that DAMGO did not evoke outward currents.

claim: The DAMGO-induced reduction of PS-evoked Ca2+ signals is unlikely to be caused by K+ channel-dependent hyperpolarization.
source: Consequently, the DAMGO-induced reduction of PS-evoked Ca2+ signals observed in Ca2+ imaging experiments (e.g. in Figure 1a–g) is unlikely to be caused by K+ channel-dependent hyperpolarization.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that DAMGO did not activate K+ channels (outward currents).

claim: TRPM3 channels in DRG neurons are inhibited by activating µORs.
source: Together, these data argue that TRPM3 channels in DRG neurons are inhibited by activating µORs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: 91.5% (562 of 614) of the PS-sensitive neurons were inhibited by DAMGO.
source: Overall, 91.5% (562 of 614) of the PS-sensitive neurons were inhibited by DAMGO.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2i, which shows the number of cells in each subgroup.

claim: Most neurons (465 of 562 cells, 83%), which showed a reduction of TRPM3-dependent Ca2+ signals due to application of DAMGO, also showed capsaicin-induced Ca2+ signals, demonstrating the presence of functional TRPV1 channels.
source: In agreement with this, we found that most neurons (465 of 562 cells, 83%), which showed a reduction of TRPM3-dependent Ca2+ signals due to application of DAMGO, also showed capsaicin-induced Ca2+ signals, demonstrating the presence of functional TRPV1 channels.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2i, which shows the number of cells in each subgroup.

claim: Only a minority of the cells without apparent effect of DAMGO on TRPM3-dependent Ca2+ signals (14 of 52 DAMGO-insensitive cells, i.e. 27% of the DAMGO-insensitive cells, corresponding to 2% of all PS-sensitive cells) showed a response to capsaicin.
source: Conversely, only a minority of the cells without apparent effect of DAMGO on TRPM3-dependent Ca2+ signals (14 of 52 DAMGO-insensitive cells, i.e. 27% of the DAMGO-insensitive cells, corresponding to 2% of all PS-sensitive cells) showed a response to capsaicin (Figure 2i).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2i, which shows the number of cells in each subgroup.

claim: Activation of µORs is capable of rapidly and strongly reducing currents through TRPM3 channels in a subset of DRG neurons, corresponding largely, but not exclusively, to putative peptidergic nociceptors.
source: Together, these data show that activation of µORs is capable of rapidly and strongly reducing currents through TRPM3 channels in a subset of DRG neurons, corresponding largely, but not exclusively, to putative peptidergic nociceptors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing the correlation between DAMGO sensitivity and capsaicin sensitivity.

claim: All GPCRs that couple to Gi/o proteins inhibited TRPM3-dependent Ca2+ signals in DRG neurons.
source: We therefore tested other GPCRs that couple to Gαi-containing G proteins and found that all of them inhibited TRPM3-dependent Ca2+ signals in DRG neurons, although the number of neurons responding to the specific agonists was variable (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3, which shows experimental measurements with various GPCR agonists.

claim: TRPM3 was inhibited by activating GABAB receptors.
source: Specifically, we found that TRPM3 was inhibited by activating GABAB receptors, CB2 cannabinoid receptors, δ-opioid receptors, adrenoreceptors and somatostatin receptors (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: TRPM3 was inhibited by activating CB2 cannabinoid receptors.
source: Specifically, we found that TRPM3 was inhibited by activating GABAB receptors, CB2 cannabinoid receptors, δ-opioid receptors, adrenoreceptors and somatostatin receptors (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: TRPM3 was inhibited by activating δ-opioid receptors.
source: Specifically, we found that TRPM3 was inhibited by activating GABAB receptors, CB2 cannabinoid receptors, δ-opioid receptors, adrenoreceptors and somatostatin receptors (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: TRPM3 was inhibited by activating adrenoreceptors.
source: Specifically, we found that TRPM3 was inhibited by activating GABAB receptors, CB2 cannabinoid receptors, δ-opioid receptors, adrenoreceptors and somatostatin receptors (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: TRPM3 was inhibited by activating somatostatin receptors.
source: Specifically, we found that TRPM3 was inhibited by activating GABAB receptors, CB2 cannabinoid receptors, δ-opioid receptors, adrenoreceptors and somatostatin receptors (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: When metabotropic glutamate type five receptors (mGluR5) were activated, the weakest inhibition of all agonists was observed, which was only detectable in a relatively small number of neurons.
source: When we activated metabotropic glutamate type five receptors (mGluR5), which preferentially couple to Gαq proteins (Bhave et al., 2001) we observed the weakest inhibition of all agonists, which was only detectable in a relatively small number of neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3f, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: The weak inhibition caused by DHPG did not recover upon washout.
source: In addition, the weak inhibition caused by DHPG did not recover upon washout (Figure 3f).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3f, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: The activity of TRPM3 channels can be inhibited by a large variety of Gαi-coupled GPCRs.
source: These data show that the activity of TRPM3 channels can be inhibited by a large variety of Gαi-coupled GPCRs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that multiple Gαi-coupled GPCRs inhibit TRPM3 channels.

claim: Ca2+ signals induced by the TRPV1 agonist capsaicin showed the same reduction in activity whether DAMGO or the solvent control (DMSO) was applied to the DRG neurons.
source: Ca2+ signals induced by the TRPV1 agonist capsaicin showed the same reduction in activity whether DAMGO or the solvent control (DMSO) was applied to the DRG neurons (Figure 4a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4a,b, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: When DAMGO was co-applied together with longer applied capsaicin, there was a much weaker inhibition compared to the inhibition typically observed with TRPM3.
source: Furthermore, when we used a different protocol and co-applied DAMGO together with longer applied capsaicin, there was a much weaker inhibition compared to the inhibition typically observed with TRPM3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: AITC-induced Ca2+ signals were not subject to inhibition by DAMGO, regardless of whether the neurons were PS-sensitive or not.
source: Similarly to our results with TRPV1, we observed that AITC-induced Ca2+ signals were not subject to inhibition by DAMGO, regardless of whether the neurons were PS-sensitive or not (Figure 4c,d).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4c,d, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: In HEK cells overexpressing TRPV1 channels together with µORs, there was no evidence for any inhibitory action of µORs on TRPV1 channels in the time frame investigated (2 min).
source: When we overexpressed TRPV1 channels together with µORs in HEK cells, we found no evidence for any inhibitory action of µORs on TRPV1 channels in the time frame investigated (2 min; Figure 4e).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4e, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: In overexpression systems, there was no indication of inhibitory action of µORs on TRPA1 channels.
source: Similarly, we investigated the coupling of µORs to TRPA1 and TRPM8 channels in overexpression systems, again without finding any indication of inhibitory action of µORs on these channels (Figure 4f,g).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4f, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: In overexpression systems, there was no indication of inhibitory action of µORs on TRPM8 channels.
source: Similarly, we investigated the coupling of µORs to TRPA1 and TRPM8 channels in overexpression systems, again without finding any indication of inhibitory action of µORs on these channels (Figure 4f,g).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4g, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: From the group of TRP channels implicated in noxious thermoreception and inflammatory hyperalgesia, only TRPM3 channels displayed a substantial, rapid and reversible inhibition during µOR activation.
source: In summary, from the group of TRP channels implicated in noxious thermoreception and inflammatory hyperalgesia, only TRPM3 channels displayed a substantial, rapid and reversible inhibition during µOR activation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that TRPV1, TRPA1, and TRPM8 channels were not substantially inhibited by µOR activation, while TRPM3 channels were.

claim: PTX treatment strongly reduced the action of DAMGO on PS-evoked activity in DRG neurons.
source: We tested whether Gi/o proteins were involved in the functional coupling of µORs to TRPM3 channels by incubating cultured DRG neurons for 16–24 hr with pertussis toxin (PTX), which selectively disrupts signaling via Gi/o proteins (Mangmool and Kurose, 2011). We found that this treatment strongly reduced the action of DAMGO on PS-evoked activity in DRG neurons (Figure 5a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5a,b, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: In HEK cells overexpressing µORs and TRPM3 proteins, PTX treatment almost completely abrogated the DAMGO-induced inhibition of TRPM3 channels.
source: Moreover, in HEK cells overexpressing µORs and TRPM3 proteins, PTX treatment almost completely abrogated the DAMGO-induced inhibition of TRPM3 channels (Figure 5c,d).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5c,d, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: The classical signaling pathway comprising G proteins containing Gαi/o subunits is strongly implicated in the inhibition of TRPM3.
source: These data strongly implicate the classical signaling pathway comprising G proteins containing Gαi/o subunits in the inhibition of TRPM3.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that PTX, which disrupts Gi/o signaling, reduces the inhibition of TRPM3 by µOR activation.

claim: Application of forskolin together with IBMX did not prevent the action of DAMGO in isolated DRG neurons.
source: We found that application of IBMX (to inhibit cAMP-degrading phosphodiesterases) and forskolin (to stimulate cAMP-producing adenylyl cyclases) did not influence TRPM3 channel activity in DRG neurons nor their inhibition by µOR activation (Figure 5e,f).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5e,f, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: Combined application of forskolin and IBMX did not influence TRPM3 channel activity in TRPM3- and µOR-overexpressing HEK cells nor their inhibition by µOR activation.
source: We observed the same outcome in TRPM3- and µOR-overexpressing HEK cells after combined application of forskolin and IBMX (Figure 5g,h).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5g,h, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: When TRPM3- and µOR-expressing HEK cells were dialyzed with the unhydrolyzable ATP analog AMP-PNP through the pipette in patch-clamp experiments, there was no evidence that this treatment affected the inhibitory action of µOR activation on TRPM3 channels.
source: However, when we dialyzed TRPM3- and µOR-expressing HEK cells with the unhydrolyzable ATP analog AMP-PNP through the pipette in patch-clamp experiments, effectively blocking the action of all kinases, including PKAs, we found no evidence that this treatment affected the inhibitory action of µOR activation on TRPM3 channels (Figure 5i,k).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5i,k, which shows electrophysiological recordings.

claim: When Mg2+ ions were removed from the intracellular solution, the inhibiting action of DAMGO on TRPM3 channel activity was lost after 5 min of internally dialyzing the cells via the patch pipette.
source: On the other hand, when we removed Mg2+ ions from the intracellular solution, the inhibiting action of DAMGO on TRPM3 channel activity was lost after 5 min of internally dialyzing the cells via the patch pipette (Figure 5j,k and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a)
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5j,k and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a, which shows electrophysiological recordings.

claim: µOR-mediated TRPM3 inhibition relies on G-protein signaling as G proteins need Mg2+ ions to bind GTP.
source: These data also support our earlier conclusion that µOR-mediated TRPM3 inhibition relies on G-protein signaling as G proteins need Mg2+ ions to bind GTP (Gilman, 1987).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that removing Mg2+ ions abolishes the inhibition, combined with the knowledge that G proteins need Mg2+ to bind GTP.

claim: Kinases are not involved in the signaling pathway of µORs to TRPM3 channels.
source: Therefore, these experiments suggest that kinases are not involved in the signaling pathway of µORs to TRPM3 channels.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that blocking kinases with AMP-PNP did not affect the inhibition of TRPM3 by µOR activation.

claim: None of the pharmacological kinase inhibitors (H89, KT5720, BIM) abolished the inhibition of TRPM3 channels by µOR activation.
source: This conclusion was further corroborated by experiments using kinase inhibitors (H89, a relatively non-specific kinase inhibitor (Lochner and Moolman, 2006); KT5720, inhibitor of PKA; BIM, inhibitor of PKC), none of which abolished the inhibition of TRPM3 channels by µOR activation (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6, which shows experimental measurements with kinase inhibitors.

claim: TRPM3 inhibition after µOR activation is a G-protein-coupled process, but does not involve the second messenger cAMP or downstream kinases.
source: Taken together, these data (Figures 5 and 6, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) strongly indicate that TRPM3 inhibition after µOR activation is a G-protein-coupled process, but does not involve the second messenger cAMP or downstream kinases.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that manipulating cAMP levels and blocking kinases did not affect the inhibition of TRPM3 by µOR activation.

claim: Overexpression of each of the three Gαi proteins, either in wild-type form or as constitutively active QtoL mutant of Gαi1, had no inhibitory effect on the activity of TRPM3 channels.
source: We overexpressed Gα or Gβγ subunits together with TRPM3 channels in HEK cells and assessed their activity by applying PS. Overexpression of each of the three Gαi proteins, either in wild-type form (Figure 7a), or as constitutively active QtoL mutant (Graziano and Gilman, 1989) of Gαi1 (Figure 7b) had no inhibitory effect on the activity of TRPM3 channels.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7a,b, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: YFP-tagged Gαi subunits failed to inhibit TRPM3 channels.
source: We also tested YFP-tagged Gαi subunits (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a), because these allowed to easily assess the expression of the proteins by fluorescence microscopy. These tagged Gαi subunits also failed to inhibit TRPM3 channels.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1a, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: Overexpression of Gαo1 did not affect PS-induced TRPM3 channel activity.
source: Equally to the Gαi subunits, overexpression of Gαo1 (Figure 7c) or Gαo2 (Figure 7d) did not affect PS-induced TRPM3 channel activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7c, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: Overexpression of Gαo2 did not affect PS-induced TRPM3 channel activity.
source: Equally to the Gαi subunits, overexpression of Gαo1 (Figure 7c) or Gαo2 (Figure 7d) did not affect PS-induced TRPM3 channel activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7d, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: Overexpression of Gαq proteins did not reduce the TRPM3-evoked Ca2+ signals.
source: Finally, also overexpression of Gαq proteins, which recently have been shown to influence TRPM8 channels (Zhang et al., 2012), did not reduce the TRPM3-evoked Ca2+ signals (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1b, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: When Gβ1 and Gγ2 proteins were overexpressed together with TRPM3 channels, TRPM3-dependent Ca2+ signals were strongly reduced.
source: However, when we overexpressed Gβ1 and Gγ2 proteins together with TRPM3 channels, TRPM3-dependent Ca2+ signals were strongly reduced (Figure 7e).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7e, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: The reduction of TRPM3 activity by Gβγ subunits was attenuated by the additional overexpression of (myristoylated) myr-βARKct, a Gβγ-binding peptide.
source: Importantly, the reduction of TRPM3 activity by Gβγ subunits was attenuated by the additional overexpression of (myristoylated) myr-βARKct (Koch et al., 1994; Rishal et al., 2005), a Gβγ-binding peptide, indicating that the inhibition of TRPM3 channels was caused specifically by the overexpressed Gβγ subunits in an unbound state (Figure 7f,g).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7f,g, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: A suppression of TRPM3 activity by overexpressed Gβγ subunits could also be demonstrated in whole-cell patch-clamp recordings of transfected HEK cells.
source: A suppression of TRPM3 activity by overexpressed Gβγ subunits could also be demonstrated in whole-cell patch-clamp recordings of transfected HEK cells (Figure 7h,i).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7h,i, which shows electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The peptide mSIRK caused a significant reduction in TRPM3 activity in DRG neurons.
source: Using this approach, we observed a significant reduction in TRPM3 activity in DRG neurons as well as in TRPM3 overexpressing HEK cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 3, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: The peptide mSIRK caused a significant reduction in TRPM3 activity in TRPM3 overexpressing HEK cells.
source: Using this approach, we observed a significant reduction in TRPM3 activity in DRG neurons as well as in TRPM3 overexpressing HEK cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 3, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: The inactive analog mSIRK-L9A did not cause a reduction in TRPM3 activity.
source: The inactive analog mSIRK-L9A did not cause this effect.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 3, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: When Gβγ-binding peptides (myr-βARKct or myr-phosducin) were overexpressed, the inhibitory signaling from µORs to TRPM3 channels was severely reduced.
source: When we tried to manipulate the concentration of free Gβγ subunits in the opposite direction by overexpression of Gβγ-binding peptides, myr-βARKct as before or myr-phosducin (Schulz, 2001; Rishal et al., 2005), we found that the inhibitory signaling from µORs to TRPM3 channels was severely reduced (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 2, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: TRPM3 channels are inhibited by free Gβγ dimers, but not by Gαi/o subunits.
source: In aggregate, these data strongly suggest a model in which TRPM3 channels are inhibited by free Gβγ dimers, but not by Gαi/o subunits.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that overexpression of Gβγ inhibits TRPM3, while overexpression of Gα subunits does not, and that scavenging Gβγ reduces the inhibition.

claim: Fused tags (YFP or myc) on TRPM3 proteins do not interfere with the functional coupling of µORs to TRPM3 channels, irrespective of their N- or C-terminal location.
source: In control experiments, we determined that fused tags (YFP or myc) on TRPM3 proteins do not interfere with the functional coupling of µORs to TRPM3 channels, irrespective of their N- or C-terminal location (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 1, which shows experimental measurements.

claim: The immunoprecipitation procedure precipitated full-length TRPM3 proteins.
source: After separating the precipitated proteins, we observed a single band in western blots at the molecular weight expected for myc-TRPM3-YFP using antibodies against GFP, indicating that our procedure indeed precipitated full-length TRPM3 proteins (Figure 8a).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 8a, which shows a western blot.

claim: Gβ co-precipitated with TRPM3 from HEK-TRPM3 cells.
source: When we probed blots with antibodies against Gβ subunits, we found evidence for Gβ co-precipitating with TRPM3 from HEK-TRPM3 cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 8b,c, which shows western blots.

claim: Using the same protocol on HEK cells without TRPM3 did not lead to precipitation of Gβ proteins.
source: Using the same protocol on HEK cells without TRPM3 did not lead to precipitation of Gβ proteins (Figure 8b,c, Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 8b,c and Figure 8—figure supplement 2, which shows western blots.

claim: In mass spectrometry experiments, peptide fragments belonging unequivocally to Gβ1 proteins were identified.
source: Finally, in order to ascertain the identity of Gβ proteins interacting with TRPM3 without the potentially confounding issue of antibody specificity, we identified in mass spectrometry experiments peptide fragments belonging unequivocally to Gβ1 proteins. These peptides originated from trypsin-digested SDS gels containing proteins co-immunoprecipitating with TRPM3 from HEK-TRPM3 cells (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 9, which shows mass spectrometry data.

claim: Gαi3 subunits were abundantly present in the cell lysates, but could not be detected on western blots of proteins co-precipitating with TRPM3.
source: Although Gαi3 subunits were abundantly present in the cell lysates, we could not detect them on western blots of proteins co-precipitating with TRPM3 (Figure 8d; see also Figure 8—figure supplement 3a for tests of the antibodies against Gαi3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 8d and Figure 8—figure supplement 3a, which shows western blots.

claim: Gαq proteins were not detected co-precipitating with TRPM3.
source: Because TRPM8 proteins have recently been shown to interact directly with Gαq proteins (Zhang et al., 2012), we also tested for, but failed to detect Gαq proteins co-precipitating with TRPM3 (Figure 8e).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 8e, which shows western blots.

claim: TRPM3 and Gβ proteins are present in the same protein complexes.
source: These data show that TRPM3 and Gβ proteins are present in the same protein complexes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry data showing that Gβ proteins co-precipitate with TRPM3.

claim: The presence of TRPM3 and Gβ proteins in the same protein complexes provides a mechanistic explanation for the inhibitory action of µORs exerted on TRPM3 channels.
source: This provides a mechanistic explanation for the inhibitory action of µORs exerted on TRPM3 channels.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry data showing that TRPM3 and Gβ proteins are in the same complex, combined with the functional data showing that Gβγ inhibits TRPM3.

claim: Co-injection of DAMGO to activate peripheral µORs strongly reduced the nocifensive behavior evoked by PS injection.
source: Co-injection of DAMGO to activate peripheral µORs (Stein and Lang, 2009) strongly reduced the nocifensive behavior evoked by PS injection, but did not affect the TRPV1-dependent pain after capsaicin injection (Figure 10a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 10a, which shows behavioral measurements in mice.

claim: Co-injection of DAMGO did not affect the TRPV1-dependent pain after capsaicin injection.
source: Co-injection of DAMGO to activate peripheral µORs (Stein and Lang, 2009) strongly reduced the nocifensive behavior evoked by PS injection, but did not affect the TRPV1-dependent pain after capsaicin injection (Figure 10a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 10b, which shows behavioral measurements in mice.

claim: Injecting higher concentrations of capsaicin into the hind paw produced considerably longer responses.
source: Injecting higher concentrations of capsaicin into the hind paw produced considerably longer responses, showing that the lower capsaicin dose used in Figure 10b did not saturate the pain-evoked behavior under our conditions (Figure 10c).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 10c, which shows behavioral measurements in mice.

claim: Co-injecting DAMGO was ineffective in reducing the duration of the capsaicin-induced nocifensive behavior at higher capsaicin doses.
source: Again, co-injecting DAMGO was ineffective in reducing the duration of the capsaicin-induced nocifensive behavior at these higher capsaicin doses (Figure 10c).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 10c, which shows behavioral measurements in mice.

claim: Locally, in the peripheral skin of living mice, TRPM3 channels, much more than TRPV1 channels, are under rapid inhibitory control of µORs.
source: These data show that locally, in the peripheral skin of living mice, TRPM3 channels, much more than TRPV1 channels, are under rapid inhibitory control of µORs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the behavioral data showing that DAMGO reduces PS-induced pain but not capsaicin-induced pain.

claim: TRPM3 channels are a major target of an intracellular signaling cascade initiated by activated µORs.
source: We show here that TRPM3 channels, expressed in primary nociceptive neurons, are a major target of an intracellular signaling cascade initiated by activated µORs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that µOR activation strongly inhibits TRPM3 channels.

claim: TRPM3 channels are inhibited by activated µORs strongly, rapidly and, reversibly.
source: TRPM3 channels are inhibited by activated µORs strongly, rapidly and, reversibly (Figures 1 and 2a–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figures 1 and 2a-c.

claim: The combined data from pharmacological experiments, overexpression studies and biochemical interaction analyses strongly suggest a model in which TRPM3 channel complexes are inhibited by directly binding to Gβγ dimers, but not to Gα subunits.
source: Mechanistically, the combined data from pharmacological experiments, overexpression studies and biochemical interaction analyses presented here strongly suggest a model in which TRPM3 channel complexes are inhibited by directly binding to Gβγ dimers, but not to Gα subunits.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that overexpression of Gβγ inhibits TRPM3, while overexpression of Gα subunits does not, and that TRPM3 and Gβ proteins are in the same complex.

claim: Binding to Gβγ is the mechanism with which µORs affect many other ion channels, like voltage-gated Ca2+ and GIRK channels.
source: Binding to Gβγ is the mechanism with which µORs affect many other ion channels, like voltage-gated Ca2+ and GIRK channels (Bourinet et al., 1996; Law et al., 2000; Marker et al., 2005; Heinke et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bourinet et al., 1996; Law et al., 2000; Marker et al., 2005; and Heinke et al., 2011.

claim: In the family of TRP ion channels, direct regulation by Gβγ appears not to be common.
source: In the family of TRP ion channels, however, direct regulation by Gβγ appears not to be common.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that only a few TRP channels have been reported to be regulated by Gβγ.

claim: One report linked TRPA1 channel activation to Gβγ dimers liberated after activation of the GPCR MrgprA3.
source: One report linked TRPA1 channel activation to Gβγ dimers liberated after activation of the GPCR MrgprA3 (Wilson et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wilson et al., 2011.

claim: µOR activation has neither an inhibition nor a pronounced activation effect on TRPA1 channels.
source: We tested therefore, whether µOR activation has an effect on TRPA1 channels in DRG neurons, but observed neither an inhibition nor a pronounced activation of these channels.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text.

claim: The only other TRP channel that has been reported to be regulated by Gβγ dimers is TRPM1.
source: The only other TRP channel that has been reported to be regulated by Gβγ dimers is TRPM1 (Shen et al., 2012), the channel protein with the highest homology to TRPM3.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Shen et al., 2012.

claim: TRPM1 is not known to be expressed in somatosensory neurons.
source: TRPM1, however, is not known to be expressed in somatosensory neurons.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about TRPM1 expression.

claim: The assertion that TRPM1 is inhibited by Gβγ dimers has been controversial since earlier work reported that purified Gβγ dimers are ineffective, while Gαo proteins inhibit heterologously expressed TRPM1.
source: The assertion that TRPM1 is inhibited by Gβγ dimers has been controversial since earlier work reported that purified Gβγ dimers are ineffective, while Gαo proteins inhibit heterologously expressed TRPM1 (Koike et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Koike et al., 2010.

claim: A recent publication provides evidence that both G protein subunits bind to TRPM1 and inhibit the channel.
source: A recent publication apparently reconciles these findings by providing evidence that both G protein subunits bind to TRPM1 and inhibit the channel (Xu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Xu et al., 2016.

claim: TRPM8 has been shown to directly bind Gαq proteins and to be strongly inhibited by this event.
source: In addition to the proposed regulation of TRPM1 by Gαo proteins, TRPM8 has recently been shown to directly bind Gαq proteins and to be strongly inhibited by this event (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2012.

claim: TRPM3 does not bind to Gα subunits.
source: Our data indicate that neither is the case (Figures 7 and 8), reinforcing our model that the main signaling pathway from µOR to TRPM3 channels is via Gβγ proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: TRPM3 is not regulated by Gα subunits.
source: Our data indicate that neither is the case (Figures 7 and 8), reinforcing our model that the main signaling pathway from µOR to TRPM3 channels is via Gβγ proteins.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: A PI3Kγ/NO pathway has been described for the stimulation of KATP channels, where PI3Kγ is activated by Gβγ subunits.
source: A PI3Kγ/NO pathway has been described for the stimulation of KATP channels, where PI3Kγ is activated by Gβγ subunits (Cunha et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cunha et al., 2010.

claim: GIRK2 channels activated directly by Gβγ proteins have been implicated in peripheral opioid analgesia.
source: Also, GIRK2 channels activated directly by Gβγ proteins have been implicated in peripheral opioid analgesia (Nockemann et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nockemann et al., 2013.

claim: GIRK2 channels are absent from mouse DRG neurons, but may play a role in human anti-nociception.
source: These channels are absent from mouse DRG neurons, but may play a role in human anti-nociception (Nockemann et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nockemann et al., 2013.

claim: Other ion channels seem to be regulated by peripheral µORs via their effects on the cellular cAMP level, often through subsequently influencing PKA activity.
source: Other ion channels seem to be regulated by peripheral µORs via their effects on the cellular cAMP level, often through subsequently influencing PKA activity (Ingram and Williams, 1994; Gold and Levine, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ingram and Williams, 1994 and Gold and Levine, 1996.

claim: TRPV1 channels are regulated by µORs through the well-established cAMP/PKA pathway.
source: Notably, TRPV1 channels are also regulated by µORs through the well-established cAMP/PKA pathway (Vetter et al., 2006; Endres-Becker et al., 2007; Vetter et al., 2008; Spahn et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vetter et al., 2006; Endres-Becker et al., 2007; Vetter et al., 2008; and Spahn et al., 2013.

claim: An entirely different, β-arrestin2-dependent pathway leading from µOR stimulation to TRPV1 activation has also been proposed.
source: An entirely different, β-arrestin2-dependent pathway leading from µOR stimulation to TRPV1 activation has also been proposed (Rowan et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rowan et al., 2014.

claim: TRPM3 channels were largely unaffected by attempts to manipulate intracellular cAMP levels.
source: Remarkably, and in stark contrast to the published regulation of TRPV1 by cAMP/PKA (Huang et al., 2006), TRPM3 channels were largely unaffected by our attempts to manipulate intracellular cAMP levels (Figure 5e–h).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5e-h.

claim: TRPM3-dependent pain (evoked by the injection of PS into the hind-paw) was strongly suppressed by concomitant injection of µOR agonists.
source: TRPM3-dependent pain (evoked by the injection of PS into the hind-paw) was strongly suppressed by concomitant injection of µOR agonists, while these substances did not significantly attenuate TRPV1-dependent pain due to the injection of capsaicin at any of the concentrations tested (Figure 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 10.

claim: µOR agonists did not significantly attenuate TRPV1-dependent pain due to the injection of capsaicin at any of the concentrations tested.
source: TRPM3-dependent pain (evoked by the injection of PS into the hind-paw) was strongly suppressed by concomitant injection of µOR agonists, while these substances did not significantly attenuate TRPV1-dependent pain due to the injection of capsaicin at any of the concentrations tested (Figure 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 10.

claim: The strong and direct functional influence of activated µORs on TRPM3 channels also works in peripheral endings of primary nociceptive neurons in vivo.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that the strong and direct functional influence of activated µORs on TRPM3 channels also works in peripheral endings of primary nociceptive neurons in vivo.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the behavioral data showing that DAMGO reduces PS-induced pain in vivo.

claim: TRPM3 channels play an important role in the physiological control of nociceptor excitability.
source: Our findings establish TRPM3 channels as privileged target of peripheral µORs and thus indicate that TRPM3 channels play an important role in the physiological control of nociceptor excitability.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that TRPM3 channels are strongly inhibited by µOR activation and that this inhibition is effective in vivo.

claim: The presence of TRPM3 channels in small-diameter nociceptor neurons has been previously described.
source: The presence of TRPM3 channels in small-diameter nociceptor neurons (Vriens et al., 2011; Usoskin et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vriens et al., 2011 and Usoskin et al., 2015.

claim: TRPM3 channels have the ability to release inflammatory mediators like CGRP.
source: their ability to release inflammatory mediators like CGRP (Held et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Held et al., 2015.

claim: The results presented in this study provide further, strong support for the contention that inhibition of TRPM3 might be a viable strategy to combat pain, especially inflammatory hyperalgesia.
source: The results presented in this study provide further, strong support for this contention, because they show that TRPM3 inhibition is an important aspect of the action spectrum of µORs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that TRPM3 inhibition is an important aspect of the action spectrum of µORs.

claim: TRPM3 inhibition is an important aspect of the action spectrum of µORs.
source: because they show that TRPM3 inhibition is an important aspect of the action spectrum of µORs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that µOR activation strongly inhibits TRPM3 channels.

claim: The findings presented here help to explain the clinical effectiveness of peripherally acting or peripherally restricted µOR agonists.
source: Potentially, the findings presented here therefore help to explain the clinical effectiveness of peripherally acting or peripherally restricted µOR agonists.
evidence: The claim is speculative, suggesting a potential explanation based on the findings.

claim: Peripherally restricted µOR agonists still can exhibit pronounced and dose-limiting adverse effects, such as tolerance and constipation.
source: However, peripherally restricted µOR agonists still can exhibit pronounced and dose-limiting adverse effects, such as tolerance and constipation (Stein, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stein, 2016.

claim: Pharmacologically inhibiting TRPM3 channels directly might be a feasible alternative to the established administration of µOR agonists.
source: Pharmacologically inhibiting TRPM3 channels directly might therefore be a feasible alternative to the established administration of µOR agonists.
evidence: The claim is speculative, suggesting a potential alternative based on the findings.

claim: Given the unremarkable phenotype of TRPM3-deficient mice, when not challenged with painful stimuli, it is reasonable to hope that unwanted effects of TRPM3 inhibitors may be less limiting than those of µOR agonists.
source: Given the unremarkable phenotype of TRPM3-deficient mice, when not challenged with painful stimuli, (Vriens et al., 2011), it is reasonable to hope that unwanted effects of TRPM3 inhibitors may be less limiting than those of µOR agonists.
evidence: The claim is speculative, suggesting a potential advantage based on the phenotype of TRPM3-deficient mice.
